Identifying Threats (Part 1): Who Attacks, From Where, and How

Good evening. In Topic 2 you learned to see Kalmia the way its owner does: a list of assets, each with an owner, a location and a value. Tonight you start seeing Kalmia the way an attacker does. Topic 3 asks a new question — who or what could harm these assets, and how? — and its answer is the threat catalogue of Lab 2, which starts on Thursday.

One hour, four lessons. Lesson 1 profiles the external actors: cybercriminals, hacktivists, state-sponsored groups and opportunistic attackers. Lesson 2 looks inside: malicious insiders, negligent users, third parties and suppliers. Lesson 3 explains the five attack methods you will meet most often. Lesson 4 follows a real ransomware attack on a small Canadian manufacturer, day by day, and asks whether Kalmia would survive the same Saturday.

The one fact to remember

A threat is not dangerous by itself; it becomes a risk only where it meets a vulnerability in an asset you care about. Tonight you list the threats. Lab 1 gave you the assets; Topic 4 will give you the vulnerabilities; Lab 3 will combine the three into risks. Every threat you record tonight must point to a Kalmia asset and to the evidence that makes it relevant.

By the end of this hour you will be able to

  1. Describe the four external threat actor types — cybercriminals, hacktivists, state-sponsored groups, opportunistic attackers — by their motivation, capability, intent and targeting, and explain which of them is most relevant to a small organization and why.
  2. Explain what an insider is, distinguish malicious insiders, negligent or accidental users, and third parties and suppliers, and recognize insider indicators without turning them into accusations.
  3. Explain how malware, ransomware, phishing and social engineering, denial of service and credential theft work, name the CIA (Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability) property each one violates, and show how they chain into one attack.
  4. Analyse a real, recent ransomware attack on a small organization from public sources, separate what is known from what is not, and compare its lessons with Kalmia's documented state.

Kalmia in one paragraph (reminder from Class 1)

Torréfaction Kalmia inc. — Kalmia Coffee Roasters Inc. — is a fictional coffee roaster founded in 2014: roastery, office and warehouse in Saint-Laurent (Montréal), three cafés (Plateau-Mont-Royal, Old Montréal, Laval), 46 employees, about $6.8 million of revenue (cafés 40%, wholesale to about 140 clients 35%, web shop and subscriptions 25%, with a third of online revenue in November and December). Nadia Roy is President and CEO (chief executive officer) and the risk owner; Karim Haddad runs operations; Sophie Tremblay runs finance and HR (human resources); Lucas Martin is the half-time IT (information technology) coordinator. InfoNord MSP (managed service provider) manages the firewall, patches the server and runs the helpdesk. The roastery network is flat; NAS-01 holds the shares and its only backup disk stays connected; ROAST-PC runs Windows 10 with the vendor's remote-access tool; MFA (multi-factor authentication) protects only two Microsoft 365 administrator accounts. Recorded incidents: INC-02 (June, fake banking details, $18,400 stopped by a call-back), INC-03 (August, two-hour POS [point of sale] cloud outage), INC-04 (September, export of 18,500 loyalty records by a former supervisor's account), INC-05 (September, phishing text messages to baristas).

Before we start — three rules for tonight (Legal Notice v2.0)

All work in this course uses the fictional case organization Kalmia Coffee Roasters Inc. (Torréfaction Kalmia inc.) and the lab material provided, with explicit authorization. Unauthorized access to, or interference with, computer systems is a criminal offence — for example under the Canadian Criminal Code s. 342.1, the US (United States) Computer Fraud and Abuse Act 18 U.S.C. § 1030, EU (European Union) Directive 2013/40/EU and Spain's Ley Orgánica 10/1995 — regardless of intent. Tonight's topic adds three specific rules. Threat information is studied, never acted on: you do not visit leak sites, contact threat actors or download breach data (section 7.3). Phishing, pretexting and any other social engineering directed at a real person are prohibited in every circumstance (sections 6.3 and 7.7.3); the e-mails and messages in this module are fictional training samples. Real incidents (Ganong Bros., KNP) are discussed only from public sources, and attribution to a group is reported as the source states it, not as established fact (section 7.3).

Lesson 1 — External threat actors and their motivations

Cybercriminals, hacktivists, state-sponsored groups and opportunistic attackers — who they are, what they want, and which of them would bother Kalmia
0:04 – 0:19

Read-aloud script — 10 minutes

From assets to threats

Until Saturday you were answering one question about Kalmia: what does it own, and who can reach it? That was Lab 1. Tonight the question changes to: who or what could harm those assets, and why? The answer becomes Lab 2, the threat catalogue, which starts on Thursday. Three words need to be precise before we start. A threat is any circumstance or event that can harm an organization's operations, assets or people through unauthorized access, destruction, disclosure, modification of information or denial of service. A threat source is who or what causes it. When the source is a person or a group acting on purpose, we call it a threat actor. This wording follows the NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) glossary and NIST SP (Special Publication) 800-30, the risk-assessment guide that defines the columns of your catalogue.

NIST SP 800-30 sorts threat sources into four families: adversarial (people who intend harm), accidental (mistakes by people who mean well), structural (failures of equipment, software or environmental controls) and environmental (fire, flood, power outage, failure of an outside service). Tonight we work on the adversarial family, first outside the organization and then inside it. An external threat actor has no authorized access to Kalmia: no account, no badge, no contract. Everything this actor gets, it must take.

Four questions that profile any threat actor

A name such as “a hacker” tells an analyst nothing useful. A profile does. In this course every threat actor is described by the answers to four questions, the first from the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security and the other three from Appendix D of NIST SP 800-30:

  1. Motivation — why does it act? Money, ideology, geopolitical advantage, personal satisfaction or discontent. Motivation predicts what the actor will try to obtain.
  2. Capability — what can it do? Skills, money, time, tools and people. Capability predicts how hard the actor can push.
  3. Intent — what does it want from this organization, and how determined is it? An actor with high intent comes back after a failure.
  4. Targeting — does it choose this victim specifically, or anyone who is vulnerable? Targeting predicts whether your size protects you. Usually it does not.

In Lab 2 the last three answers are rated on the five-level scale of NIST SP 800-30 — very low (1), low (2), moderate (3), high (4), very high (5). Motivation is written in words. You do not have to guess these ratings: each one must be backed by evidence from Kalmia's documents or from a public source, and the source goes in the evidence column.

Cybercriminals

Cybercriminals attack for money. The Cyber Centre describes them as primarily financially motivated, and their sophistication varies widely from one group to another. What makes them the most frequent attackers of small companies is the way they are organized. The National Cyber Threat Assessment 2025-2026 calls it the cybercrime-as-a-service model: criminals specialize and sell services to one another. One group writes ransomware and rents it to affiliates who carry out the attacks; this is ransomware-as-a-service. Another group, the initial access broker, does nothing except break into companies and sell the access. Others sell stolen passwords collected by information-stealing malware, or kits for building fake login pages. Because each step is bought ready-made, an attack on a 46-person coffee roaster costs a criminal very little.

Kalmia has already met cybercriminals once. In June, incident INC-02: an e-mail from a domain that imitated the coffee importer's domain announced new banking details, the account was changed in Sage 50, and an $18,400 payment was stopped only because Karim Haddad called the importer on a known number. That is business email compromise (BEC), a fraud that needs no malware at all. The same family of actors would be interested in Kalmia's file server NAS-01 (ransomware), in the web shop's checkout page (card-skimming code), and in the 18,500 loyalty records (resale or extortion). The Cyber Centre's assessment is that ransomware is the top cybercrime threat to Canada's critical infrastructure, and that fraud and scams are the most common form of cybercrime affecting Canadians.

Hacktivists

Hacktivists attack to promote a political or social cause. Their motivation is ideological, and success for them means visibility: a website that does not load, a home page replaced by their message (defacement), or internal documents published online (a leak). The Cyber Centre rates them generally less sophisticated than state actors or organized criminals; many use free or rented tools. The 2025-2026 assessment calls geopolitically motivated hacktivists unpredictable and notes that pro-Russia non-state actors ran DDoS (distributed denial of service) campaigns against Government of Canada and private-sector websites in 2023.

Would anyone campaign against a coffee roaster? Two routes are realistic. Directly, if Kalmia's brand became linked to a cause — its web shop advertises “direct-trade” beans, and a dispute about a farm's labour practices could make it a target. Indirectly, as collateral, when a group floods many Canadian commercial websites during a political event. The asset at risk is the same in both cases: the availability of the web shop in November and December, when it earns a third of its yearly online revenue, and Kalmia's reputation.

State-sponsored groups

State-sponsored groups work for, or with the support of, a government. Their motivation is geopolitical: espionage, theft of intellectual property, preparation for disruption, influence, and for some states, money to fund the regime. They have the highest capability of all actors — dedicated teams, custom tools, and the patience to stay hidden inside a network for months. A long, hidden intrusion of this kind is called an advanced persistent threat (APT). The Cyber Centre names China, Russia and Iran as the greatest strategic cyber threats to Canada, and assesses China's program as the most sophisticated and active; it describes North Korea as conducting cybercrime such as ransomware and cryptocurrency theft to fund the regime, and India as building its capabilities and likely conducting espionage against Government of Canada networks.

Kalmia holds nothing a state wants: no government contracts, no defence data, no critical-infrastructure systems. Its roast profiles are valuable to a competitor, not to a foreign intelligence service. Yet the assessment describes two situations that concern small organizations directly. First, state actors exploit edge devices — routers, firewalls and VPN (virtual private network) gateways — and Chinese and Russian actors have routed attacks through compromised SOHO (small office / home office) routers in Canada and the United States, to hide where the traffic really comes from. Kalmia's three café routers are SOHO devices. Second, states compromise suppliers in order to reach their customers: a software update, a cloud service, an IT (information technology) provider. Kalmia depends on an MSP (managed service provider), InfoNord, which has administrator rights in its Microsoft 365. For Kalmia the state-sponsored actor is therefore rarely the final target but possibly a user of its equipment or a passenger in its supply chain. Note the legal rule here: we report what the Cyber Centre assesses; we never attribute an incident to a state ourselves (Legal Notice, section 7.3).

Opportunistic attackers

An opportunistic attacker does not choose a victim. It scans the whole Internet automatically for a known weakness — a camera with its factory password, a website plugin with a published vulnerability, a remote-access service with a guessable password — and attacks whoever has it. This group includes the people the Cyber Centre calls thrill-seekers, who attack for satisfaction with ready-made tools (often called script kiddies), and criminal botnets that recruit any device they can log in to. Their capability is often low and their targeting is close to zero, but their activity never stops.

The textbook case is the Mirai botnet of 2016: malware that logged in to cameras and routers with their default passwords and used hundreds of thousands of them to flood websites, as described in CISA (Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency) alert TA16-288A. Kalmia has exactly that weakness — two of its seven cameras still use their factory passwords — and four web shop plugins that have not been updated for six months. This is the most important idea of Lesson 1: you cannot change an attacker's motivation, but you can change your exposure. For an opportunistic attacker, exposure is the only selection criterion.

Professor cue Keep each actor type to about two minutes. After the table, ask: “Which of the four will most probably reach Kalmia first?” Most students answer “state hackers” or “criminals”. Lead them to “opportunistic attackers”, because the selection criterion is exposure, and Kalmia's exposure is documented in Lab 1. Do not let anyone name a real group as the author of an incident; repeat that attribution comes only from official sources.

Micro-activity — match the actor to the evidence (2 min)

Four short facts appear on the slide. For each one, the class answers out loud: which actor type, and which motivation? (1) A supplier's “new banking details” arrive from a look-alike domain. (2) The web shop goes offline on the day of a national political announcement, together with forty other Canadian shops. (3) A café router is found relaying traffic for a foreign intrusion campaign. (4) A camera that kept its factory password joins a botnet.

Answer key (1) cybercriminal — financial (BEC); (2) hacktivist — ideological, collateral DDoS; (3) state-sponsored — geopolitical, Kalmia used as a relay, not targeted (we would report such a finding to the Cyber Centre and let it attribute); (4) opportunistic — easy win; the only selection criterion was the default password. Insist on the reason for each answer, not the label.

Real-life example — Who would attack Kalmia, and why? — the external threat-source profiles

Real-life example 1 · Kalmia Coffee Roasters Inc. (fictional)

Who would attack Kalmia, and why? — the external threat-source profiles

Task. Build one profile for each of the four external actor types, using Kalmia's documented facts (assets, exposure, incidents, business calendar) and official public sources: motivation in words, capability, intent and targeting on the 1–5 scale of NIST SP 800-30, the number of Kalmia weaknesses that match the actor's usual methods (exposure match), the Kalmia assets the actor would want, and the evidence for every rating.
How it relates to the lecture. This is Lesson 1 applied: the four profiling questions become the columns of a table, and every rating is tied to a fact. The example also shows the central idea of the lesson — an actor with low skill and no interest in Kalmia can still be the most relevant one, because of exposure.
Labs it prepares. Lab 2 — Threat catalogue (starts Thursday, November 5): the four rows are the starter of the section “External threat sources”; the CSV (comma-separated values) file written by the script can be pasted into the Lab 2 workbook. Lab 3 — Risk register: capability, intent and targeting feed the likelihood rating of each risk. Integrative Project, section 3.

Lucas Martin's interview (Class 1), the Lab 1 inventory and Kalmia's incident notes give twelve facts that matter to an attacker. The analyst matches them against what attracts each actor type. The result is below; the code that follows computes the same table step by step.

Read the last two columns together. The state-sponsored row has the highest capability and the lowest intent: Kalmia is not a target, but its routers could be borrowed, so the row stays in the catalogue with “relevance: moderate”. The opportunistic row has low capability and no targeting at all, yet it ranks high, because three of Kalmia's documented weaknesses are exactly what automated scans look for. Relevance is a course convention to decide which rows deserve attention first in Lab 2; it is not yet a likelihood. Likelihood is rated in Topic 5, when the vulnerabilities of Topic 4 are known.

Code example 1 — External threat-source profiler (Python)

Task. A Python script that reads two data files — Kalmia's twelve attacker-relevant facts and the profiles of the four external actor types — and, for each actor, computes intent and targeting from the facts that attract it, counts the documented weaknesses that match its usual methods, assigns a relevance level, prints each decision, and writes threat_sources_external.csv for Lab 2.
How it relates to the lecture. It turns the four profiling questions of Lesson 1 into a repeatable procedure: the same facts always give the same ratings, and every rating keeps its evidence. The bubble chart shows the result as it is computed — capability on the horizontal axis, intent on the vertical axis, exposure match as the bubble size.
▶ Interactive run — use Start / Pause, Step and Restart inside the window
Data files:
Show the complete commented code — kalmia_threat_sources.py (Python; a comment line above every line of code)
Step-by-step explanation
  1. The script imports the csv module (to read and write the data files) and Path (to build file names that work on Windows, macOS and Linux).
  2. It reads kalmia_facts.csv into a dictionary: each fact identifier (F01 … F12) points to a row that says whether the fact is present at Kalmia and gives the evidence.
  3. It reads actor_profiles.csv: one row per actor type, with its motivation, its capability, a base intent, a base targeting, the facts that attract it (with a weight) and the facts that match its usual methods.
  4. For each actor, intent starts at the base value and each attracting fact present at Kalmia adds its weight; the result is kept between 1 and 5. A negative weight (for example “no data of state interest”) lowers intent.
  5. Targeting starts at the base value and rises by one for each fact that gives a reason to pick Kalmia specifically (the holiday-season pressure, a backup that would make paying more likely, a public stance).
  6. Exposure match counts the facts that correspond to the actor's usual methods; relevance is High when intent ≥ 4 with capability ≥ 3, or exposure match ≥ 3; Moderate when intent ≥ 3 or exposure match ≥ 2; otherwise Low.
  7. Each decision is printed in the execution window; the bubble of the actor appears on the chart with its colour (red High, amber Moderate, green Low).
  8. Finally the script writes threat_sources_external.csv — the four rows of the starter catalogue with their evidence — and prints a summary. Start/Pause, Step and Restart replay the recorded run line by line; Copy copies the full commented source.
Run it yourself: install Python 3.10 or later, put kalmia_threat_sources.py, kalmia_facts.csv and actor_profiles.csv in one folder of your lab machine, open a terminal in that folder and type python kalmia_threat_sources.py (on macOS or Linux: python3 kalmia_threat_sources.py). The file threat_sources_external.csv appears next to the script.

Lesson 2 — Internal threats: malicious insiders, negligent users, third parties and suppliers
People who already have access — employees, former employees, contractors and suppliers — and the indicators an analyst looks for
0:19 – 0:31
Read-aloud script — 8 minutes
Who counts as an insider
An external actor has to break in. An insider does not: the access is already there. CISA (Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency) defines an insider as any person who has, or had, authorized access to or knowledge of an organization's resources — its people, facilities, information, equipment, networks and systems. An insider threat is the potential for that person to use the access or the knowledge, on purpose or by mistake, to harm the organization. Two words in the definition deserve attention. “Had” means a former employee whose account still works is an insider. “Knowledge” means that someone who knows how payments are approved is an insider even without any computer account.
CISA divides insider threats by intent. Unintentional threats come from negligence — the person knows the rule and ignores it, for example by writing a PIN (personal identification number) on a sticky note — or from an accident, an honest mistake such as sending a file to the wrong address. Intentional threats come from malicious insiders, who harm the organization on purpose. CISA adds two cases that involve outsiders: collusive threats, where an insider works with an external criminal, and third-party threats, from contractors and vendors who are not employees but have been given access to facilities, systems, networks or people. The course outline groups these into three families: malicious insiders, negligent users, and third parties and suppliers.
Malicious insiders
A malicious insider uses legitimate access to steal, to commit fraud, to sabotage or to take revenge. The Cyber Centre notes that insider threat actors are often motivated by discontent. What makes them hard to detect is that their actions look like normal work: an administrator exports a list, a supervisor issues a refund, a clerk changes a supplier record. The difference is not the action but the context — the time, the volume, the person, and whether the action was needed.
Kalmia's incident INC-04 is the clearest example. A shift supervisor left the company on July 15; her administrator account on the loyalty platform was never disabled; on September 18 at 21:47 that account exported the 18,500 member records. The export was found only on October 2, in the platform's audit log, after a customer complaint. Notice what we know and what we do not. We know that an account belonging to a former employee exported personal information. We do not know who typed the password, or why. An analyst records the facts and the indicator; the investigation decides the rest. Under Québec's private-sector privacy law, as amended by Law 25, this is a confidentiality incident: Kalmia must record it in its register and, if there is a risk of serious injury, notify the CAI (Commission d'accès à l'information du Québec) and the people concerned.
Negligent and accidental users
Most insider incidents are not malicious. A negligent user creates the opening through carelessness: a shared password, a PIN written under the cash drawer, a security warning clicked away, a sensitive file saved in a folder that everyone can read. An accidental user makes an honest mistake. These users matter in a threat catalogue for two reasons. They cause harm directly — data exposed, money sent to the wrong account — and they are the people that external attackers manipulate. INC-02 is a good example: the person who changed the importer's bank details in Sage 50 had no bad intent. An external criminal used that employee as the tool of the fraud. In a catalogue this becomes two rows: an external threat source (the fraudster) and an internal condition (a payment process that a single e-mail can change).
Kalmia's documents already show several negligent practices: each café shares one manager PIN among its shift leads; the NAS-01 administrator password is shared by four people; an HR (human resources) form was scanned into a folder that every employee can read. None of these is an attack. Each one makes an attack easier or makes it impossible to know who did what.
Third parties and suppliers
A third party is an organization or a person outside the company that receives some level of access to do its work: a managed service provider, a software vendor, a freelance developer, a cloud service, a maintenance company. When an attacker compromises the third party, the third party's access becomes the attacker's access. The Verizon 2025 DBIR (Data Breach Investigations Report) found third-party involvement in 30% of the breaches it analysed, twice the previous year's share. The Cyber Centre's assessment gives a Canadian example: in October 2023, ransomware hit the IT (information technology) provider of five Southern Ontario hospitals, and the hospitals had to shut down internal systems temporarily.
Kalmia relies on at least five third parties with access: InfoNord MSP (managed service provider), which has global administrator rights in Microsoft 365 and manages the firewall; RoastTech, the roaster's vendor, which connects to ROAST-PC through an unattended remote-access tool with a shared password and no end date; Émile Gagnon, the freelance web developer, who is a WordPress administrator without MFA (multi-factor authentication); and the cloud providers of the POS (point of sale), loyalty and payroll services. A supplier can also harm Kalmia without any attacker: incident INC-03, the two-hour POS outage in August, was a failure of a supplier's service — a structural or environmental threat source in NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) terms, not an adversarial one. And a supplier's identity can be stolen: INC-02 used the coffee importer's name. This is why supply chain risk is part of the threat catalogue.
Indicators are not proof
An indicator is an observable fact that may signal an insider threat: an account of a former employee that is still active or is used; a bulk export by someone who does not normally export; access at an unusual time; a vendor session outside the agreed window; the same person creating a supplier's bank details and releasing the payment; nine refunds in forty minutes under a shared PIN. Indicators guide the analyst; they are not accusations. In Lab 2 you record the indicator, the asset, the property of the CIA (Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability) triad at stake and the source document. In Lab 4 you propose the control — an offboarding checklist, individual PINs, approval for vendor sessions, a second person for bank-detail changes. You never name a person as guilty: that is not the analyst's role, and it would break the confidentiality rules of the course (Legal Notice, sections 7.5 and 18).
Professor cue Spend the most time on INC-04 and INC-02: the first shows a former insider, the second shows an innocent insider used by an outsider. Ask the class: “Is the shared manager PIN a threat?” Correct answer: no — it is a vulnerability that a malicious or a negligent insider can use, and it destroys accountability. Remind the class that Kalmia's people are fictional; even so, findings are worded as facts about accounts and processes, never as accusations against a person.
Key terms of Lesson 2
insider
any person who has or had authorized access to, or knowledge of, an organization's resources (CISA)
insider threat
the potential for an insider to use authorized access or knowledge to harm the organization, on purpose or by mistake
unintentional threat: negligence · accident
the person knows the rule and ignores it · an honest mistake
intentional threat · malicious insider
harm caused on purpose · an insider who steals, defrauds, sabotages or takes revenge
collusive threat
an insider working with an external actor
third party · third-party threat
an outside organization or person given access to do its work · harm through that access, or through the compromise of that party
supply chain
the suppliers, providers and products an organization depends on, including software updates and cloud services
indicator
an observable fact that may signal a threat; it guides investigation and is never proof of guilt
separation of duties
a control in which two different people must perform the steps of a sensitive task, such as changing bank details and releasing a payment
offboarding
the procedure that removes a departing person's accounts, access and equipment on the last day
Micro-activity — malicious, negligent or third party? (3 min)
Six situations from Kalmia's notes appear on the slide; the class votes for each one. (1) The account of a supervisor who left in July exports the loyalty list. (2) A barista writes the manager PIN under the cash drawer. (3) RoastTech connects to ROAST-PC at 02:14 without a ticket. (4) An employee changes a supplier's bank details after a convincing e-mail. (5) The freelance developer installs a plugin downloaded from a forum. (6) An HR form is scanned into the folder that everyone can read.
Answer key (1) malicious-insider indicator — former insider, access never removed; (2) negligent user; (3) third party — session outside the agreed window, to be verified with the vendor; (4) unintentional insider manipulated by an external fraudster (BEC [business email compromise]); (5) third party and supply chain — software from an unofficial source; (6) accidental or negligent user — confidentiality exposure. Point out that (1), (3) and (5) are indicators to investigate, not proof.

Real-life example 2 · Kalmia Coffee Roasters Inc. (fictional)
Inside the walls — reviewing Kalmia's accounts and audit logs for insider and third-party signals
Task. Review thirteen accounts across Kalmia's systems and ten audit-log entries from September and October, apply eleven indicator rules, classify every finding as malicious-insider indicator, negligent or accidental user, or third party and supplier, and record for each one the evidence, the CIA property at stake, the threat event to enter in Lab 2 and a control idea for Lab 4.
How it relates to the lecture. This is Lesson 2 applied: the CISA categories become columns, indicators are taken from real records (accounts and logs), and each finding is worded as a fact, not an accusation.
Labs it prepares. Lab 2 — Threat catalogue: the findings feed the section “Internal threat sources and third parties” (threat source, threat event, evidence). Also note that eight of the thirteen accounts would have been harmless with three administrative controls — offboarding, named accounts and MFA — which is why Lab 4 starts there.
Code example 2 — Insider and third-party signal review (PowerShell)
Task. A PowerShell script that imports two CSV (comma-separated values) exports — accounts.csv (13 accounts from seven systems) and audit_events.csv (10 log entries) — applies eleven indicator rules, classifies each finding into one of the CISA-based categories, records the CIA property, the Lab 2 threat event and a Lab 4 control idea, prints every decision, and exports insider_findings.csv.
How it relates to the lecture. It reproduces the review of the real-life example as a procedure that Lucas Martin could run every month: the rules are the indicators of Lesson 2, and the output is worded as facts about accounts and events, never as accusations. The swim-lane drawing places each finding in its category as the script finds it.
▶ Interactive run — use Start / Pause, Step and Restart inside the window
Data files:
Show the complete commented code — Get-KalmiaInsiderSignals.ps1 (PowerShell; a comment line above every line of code)
Step-by-step explanation
  1. The script declares two parameters with default file names, so it runs without arguments in the lab folder, and sets strict mode so that a typing error in a variable name stops the script instead of producing a silent wrong result.
  2. It imports the two CSV files with Import-Csv: each row becomes an object whose properties are the column names (System, Account, Person, Type, Status, MFA, Privilege …).
  3. A small helper function, Add-Finding, builds one finding object with all the columns of the output and adds it to a list; every rule calls it, so all findings have the same shape.
  4. Account rules run first: a former employee whose account is still active (R1), a shared account or PIN (R2), a privileged account without MFA (R3), a vendor with privileged access (R4).
  5. Event rules run next on the audit log: a bulk export (R5), a vendor session outside the agreed hours or without a ticket (R6), the same person changing bank details and releasing a payment within one hour (R7), a sign-in by a former employee's account (R8), a burst of refunds under a shared PIN (R9), a sensitive file saved to a share readable by everyone (R10), software installed from an unofficial source (R11).
  6. Each finding is printed as it is found and its card drops into the matching lane of the drawing: malicious-insider indicators, negligent or accidental users, third parties and suppliers.
  7. At the end the script groups the findings by category and by CIA property, prints the totals, and exports insider_findings.csv with Export-Csv (UTF-8, no type header) for Lab 2.
  8. The execution window is a step-by-step model of the script recorded from its logic (no PowerShell interpreter runs inside this page); run the real script on any Windows computer with PowerShell 5.1 or 7 in the lab folder to obtain the same output.
Run it yourself: on the Windows lab virtual machine, put Get-KalmiaInsiderSignals.ps1, accounts.csv and audit_events.csv in one folder, open PowerShell 7 (pwsh) or Windows PowerShell 5.1 in that folder and type .\Get-KalmiaInsiderSignals.ps1. If the execution policy blocks a downloaded script, type Unblock-File .\Get-KalmiaInsiderSignals.ps1 first. The run shown in the window replays the script's logic step by step (the workspace that prepared this module has no PowerShell); the real script prints the same 17 findings and writes insider_findings.csv.

Lesson 3 — Common attack methods: malware, ransomware, phishing and social engineering, DoS, credential theft
What each method does, which CIA property it violates, what it looks like at Kalmia, and how methods chain into one attack
0:31 – 0:50
Read-aloud script — 12 minutes
Actor, method, tool
Lessons 1 and 2 answered who. Lesson 3 answers how. Keep three words apart. The threat actor is the person or group. The attack method is what the actor does — trick a person, guess a password, flood a server. The tool is what it uses — a piece of malware, a phishing kit, a botnet. In your threat catalogue the method becomes the threat event column: “ransomware encrypts NAS-01 after a phishing e-mail” is a threat event; “a ransomware group” is a threat source. In Class 5 you will give each event its identifier from MITRE ATT&CK (Adversarial Tactics, Techniques, and Common Knowledge), the public catalogue of attacker techniques; tonight you only see those identifiers as a preview.
Malware
Malware, short for malicious software, is a program inserted into a system without the owner's consent in order to compromise the confidentiality, integrity or availability of its data or of the system itself — the definition of NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) SP (Special Publication) 800-83. The families you will meet most often are the trojan, which pretends to be a useful program; the virus, which attaches to a file and spreads when the file is opened; the worm, which spreads over the network by itself; spyware and keyloggers, which collect information and keystrokes; and information stealers, which copy the passwords and session cookies saved in browsers. Malware rarely arrives by magic. It is delivered: an e-mail attachment that asks you to “enable content”, a fake software update, a USB (Universal Serial Bus) stick, a vulnerable service exposed to the Internet, or a trusted update that was tampered with at the supplier. The delivery step is what you can block.
Ransomware
Ransomware is malware that encrypts files or locks systems and demands payment for the decryption key. Modern groups add double extortion: before encrypting, they copy data out and threaten to publish it if the victim does not pay. That is why a ransomware attack today is usually a confidentiality incident as well as an availability incident. A ransomware attack is not one click; it is a sequence of stages that can take hours or weeks: initial access (a stolen password, a phishing attachment, an exposed remote-access service), escalation of privileges, discovery of the network, deletion or encryption of the backups that are reachable, copying of data, and finally encryption, usually at night or on a weekend so that nobody reacts in time.
Small organizations are the main victims. The Verizon 2025 DBIR (Data Breach Investigations Report) found ransomware in 44% of all the breaches it analysed, and in 88% of breaches at small and medium-sized businesses, against 39% at large organizations. The same report gives a median ransom payment of $115,000 and notes that 64% of victims did not pay. At Kalmia, the stages already have names: initial access through a Microsoft 365 account without MFA (multi-factor authentication) or through RoastLink; free movement on the flat roastery network; and NAS-01, whose only backup disk stays plugged in, so the backup would be encrypted together with the data.
Phishing and social engineering
Social engineering means manipulating a person into doing something that helps the attacker: clicking, opening, revealing, approving, paying. Phishing is social engineering by message. It comes in several channels: e-mail; smishing by text message; vishing by voice call; QR (Quick Response) codes that lead to a fake login page; and spear phishing, a message prepared for one person or one company with real names and details. Business email compromise, seen in Lesson 1, is spear phishing aimed at a payment. Phishing has one of three goals: make the victim run malware, make the victim type a password on a fake page, or make the victim act directly — change bank details, buy gift cards, read a PIN (personal identification number) aloud.
Every phishing message relies on the same psychological levers: urgency (“today before 3 pm”), authority (the CEO [chief executive officer], the bank, the IT [information technology] provider), fear or reward, and a familiar context so that nothing seems odd. The visible signs that follow from those levers are the red flags you will learn to spot: a sender domain that is almost right, a reply-to address that differs from the sender, a link whose real address does not match its text, an unexpected attachment that asks to enable macros, a request to bypass the normal procedure. Kalmia has two recorded cases: INC-02, the fake banking details by e-mail, and INC-05, text messages telling baristas “your schedule changed — log in here”. All the messages in this module are fictional training samples; sending phishing or pretexting messages to real people is prohibited in every circumstance (Legal Notice, sections 6.3 and 7.7.3).
Denial of service
A denial of service (DoS) makes a service unavailable to its legitimate users. A distributed denial of service (DDoS) does it from many machines at once, usually a botnet — thousands of infected computers, cameras and routers controlled remotely. Some floods simply exhaust the bandwidth; others send requests that are expensive for the server, such as searches or checkout pages. DoS attacks the availability property only: nothing is stolen and nothing is changed, but nobody can buy. They are the favourite method of hacktivists, and they are also sold as a service and used for extortion. For Kalmia the critical moment is easy to predict: a flood on the checkout page during the last week of November would stop the web shop at the time of year that brings a third of its online revenue. Not every outage is an attack, however: INC-03, the POS (point of sale) outage in August, was a supplier failure.
Credential theft
A credential is what proves an identity to a system: a password, a PIN, a session cookie, a one-time code. Credential theft is the family of methods that obtain one. Attackers guess weak passwords (password guessing or brute force); try one common password on many accounts (password spraying); replay username and password pairs leaked from other sites (credential stuffing), which works because people reuse passwords; collect them with phishing pages; or steal them with information stealers. With a valid credential the attacker does not break in — it logs in. The Play ransomware advisory of CISA (Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency), the FBI (Federal Bureau of Investigation) and Australia's ACSC (Australian Cyber Security Centre) lists the abuse of valid accounts among the usual ways that group gets into networks.
Multi-factor authentication (MFA) blocks most stolen-password attacks, because the password alone is no longer enough. Attackers answer with MFA fatigue, also called push bombing: they send approval requests again and again until the tired user taps “Approve”. The defence is to use number matching or phishing-resistant methods, and to teach users that an unexpected request means someone already has their password. At Kalmia, MFA protects only the two Microsoft 365 administrator accounts; the nine staff accounts, the loyalty administrators and the three WordPress administrators rely on a password alone.
How the methods chain together
Real attacks combine methods. A typical chain against a small company looks like this: a phishing e-mail (social engineering) leads to a fake Microsoft 365 page (credential theft); the stolen password opens the mailbox and the VPN (virtual private network); the attacker installs tools (malware), finds the file server, deletes the reachable backups, copies HR (human resources) files and launches ransomware on a Saturday night. A DDoS may even be added to increase the pressure. That is why one control can break several methods at once: MFA stops the stolen password, an offline backup removes the ransom pressure, and a person who reports the first e-mail stops everything.

Micro-activity — find the six red flags (3 min)
A fictional training e-mail appears on the slide: “From: Café Sol Importation <comptes@cafesol-importation.co> · Reply-To: payments.cafesol@outlook-mail.net · Subject: URGENT — new banking details for invoice 4471 · Attachment: Facture_4471.docm — Please update before 3 pm today; our bank changed after an audit. Click ‘Enable content’ to see the new account. Do not call, our phones are down.” Students list the red flags.
Answer key (1) look-alike sender domain (.co instead of the usual domain); (2) reply-to address different from the sender; (3) urgency (“before 3 pm today”); (4) request to change banking details by e-mail; (5) macro-enabled attachment asking to enable content; (6) discourages verification (“do not call”). Correct response: do not reply or open; call the importer on the number already in the supplier file; report to Lucas Martin. This sample is fictional and must never be sent to anyone.

Real-life example — Monday, 08:30 at Kalmia — seven alerts, five methods
Real-life example 3 · Kalmia Coffee Roasters Inc. (fictional)
Monday, 08:30 at Kalmia — seven alerts, five methods
Task. Classify seven events reported to Lucas Martin on the Monday after Black Friday: name the primary attack method (and a secondary one when methods chain), the CIA property violated, the asset, the first defensive action, and the ATT&CK technique identifier to be completed in Class 5; then write each event as one row of the Lab 2 threat-event list.
How it relates to the lecture. This is Lesson 3 applied: methods are recognized from observable facts, not from product names; one event can carry two methods (phishing that delivers malware); and every method is tied to the CIA property it violates.
Labs it prepares. Lab 2 — Threat catalogue: the seven rows are the starter of the “Threat events” section, and their ATT&CK identifiers are completed in Class 5. Lab 3 — Risk register: the events combine with Kalmia's vulnerabilities (Topic 4) into risk statements. Lab 4 — Treatment plan: the first defensive actions become candidate controls (MFA with number matching, macro blocking, offline backup, DDoS protection, call-back rule).
All seven events are fictional and were built from Kalmia's real weaknesses. The table gives the analyst's answers; Code example 3 reaches them through a decision tree and animates each attack path on Kalmia's network.
EventWhat was observedPrimary methodSecondaryCIAFirst defensive action
E1Sophie receives “Facture_4471.docm” from a look-alike domain of the importer; the document asks to “Enable content”Phishing (spear phishing)Malware (macro dropper)I, CDo not open; report; block macros from the Internet
E2Files on NAS-01 renamed *.locked; README_RESTORE.txt in every folder; the backup disk is also encryptedRansomwareDouble extortion threatenedA, CDisconnect NAS-01 from the network, keep it powered on, call the incident contact
E3Baristas receive an SMS: “Your schedule changed — log in at kalmia-horaires.com”Phishing (smishing)Credential theftCWarn staff; block the domain; reset passwords typed on the page
E4A caller claiming to be InfoNord asks the Plateau manager to read the POS manager PIN “for an update”Social engineering (vishing, pretexting)Credential theftC, IRefuse; call InfoNord back on the contract number; change the PIN
E5Checkout page: 48,000 requests per minute from about 3,000 addresses; real customers cannot payDDoS—AActivate the hosting provider's DDoS protection; contact the provider
E6WordPress: 1,240 failed logins in 10 minutes on admin, nroy and egagnon from 180 addressesCredential theft (password spraying / stuffing)—CLock or throttle logins; enforce MFA for administrators
E7Sophie receives 14 Microsoft 365 approval requests at 23:10 and approves the 15th to make them stopCredential theft (MFA fatigue)— (her password was already stolen)CRevoke sessions; reset the password; enable number matching
Three events (E3, E4, E7) end in credential theft even though they start differently — by text, by voice, by push requests. That is why “credential theft” is listed separately from phishing in the course outline: the method that obtains the credential and the use of the stolen credential are two different rows in the catalogue. E2 is the outcome that every other event can lead to, and the always-connected backup disk turns it from an incident into a crisis.
Code example 3 — Attack-method identifier and attack-path animation (self-contained HTML)
Task. A self-contained web page (HTML [HyperText Markup Language], CSS [Cascading Style Sheets] and JavaScript in one file) that takes the seven events of the Monday morning, asks five observable questions about each one in order, follows the answers to a primary and a secondary method, and animates the attack path on a drawing of Kalmia's network: a phishing envelope travelling to a mailbox, files turning red during encryption, a request-rate bar during the DDoS, a counter of failed logins, repeated MFA prompts. It writes every decision to an execution window and can export the threat-event rows as CSV (comma-separated values).
How it relates to the lecture. It illustrates the five methods of Lesson 3, the idea that methods chain (E1, E3, E4, E7), and the link between each method and the CIA property it violates. Pausing on an event lets the class discuss the question that decided the method.
▶ Interactive run — use Start / Pause, Step and Restart inside the window
Show the complete commented code — kalmia_attack_method_identifier.html (HTML / JavaScript; a comment line above every line of code)
Step-by-step explanation
  1. The page holds the seven events as data: the observed facts and the answers to five questions — did a person get manipulated? does unwanted software run? are files encrypted with a demand? is a service flooded? is a credential the target?
  2. Start runs the engine one decision at a time; each question, the answer and the branch taken are written to the execution window.
  3. The first “yes” sets the primary method; later “yes” answers become secondary methods, which shows the chains (phishing → malware, smishing → credential theft).
  4. When the method is known, the matching animation runs on the network drawing and the tally bars by method and by CIA property are updated.
  5. The event is then written as a threat-event row (method, asset, CIA, ATT&CK preview, first defensive action) in the result table.
  6. Pause stops after the current decision and Start resumes from exactly that point; Step advances one decision; Restart clears everything. Copy code copies the full commented source; the download buttons save the page, the drawing (SVG [Scalable Vector Graphics] or PNG [Portable Network Graphics]) and the threat-event rows (CSV).
Run it yourself: download the file and open it in any modern browser (Edge, Chrome, Firefox, Safari). Nothing is installed and nothing is sent anywhere; the page works offline.
Schematic 3 — Five common attack methods and how they chain into one ransomware attack
Top: the five methods with what each does, the CIA property it violates and the first defence. Bottom: a typical chain against a small company — phishing, stolen credential, malware, backup deletion, data copy, encryption — with the control that breaks each step.
Graph 1 — The threat landscape in six numbers (Verizon 2025 Data Breach Investigations Report)
Shares of the confirmed breaches analysed in the 2025 DBIR. The rust bar is the figure that concerns Kalmia most: ransomware was present in 88% of the breaches at small and medium-sized businesses, against 39% at large organizations. Hover a bar to read its value and source.
Five flash-cards — click a card to reveal the answer
What is double extortion?click to flip
The ransomware group copies data out before encrypting it, then threatens to publish it if the victim does not pay — so the attack violates confidentiality as well as availability.click to flip back
Name the channels of phishing.click to flip
E-mail, text message (smishing), voice call (vishing), QR codes, and spear phishing prepared for one target; business email compromise is spear phishing aimed at a payment.click to flip back
Which CIA property does a DDoS attack violate, and why is the last week of November critical for Kalmia?click to flip
Availability only. Kalmia's web shop earns about a third of its yearly online revenue in November and December, so a flood on the checkout page then causes the largest loss.click to flip back
What is the difference between password spraying and credential stuffing?click to flip
Spraying tries one common password on many accounts; stuffing replays username–password pairs leaked from other sites, which works because people reuse passwords.click to flip back
What is MFA fatigue, and what defeats it?click to flip
The attacker, who already has the password, sends approval requests until the user accepts one. Number matching or phishing-resistant MFA, and reporting unexpected requests, defeat it.click to flip back

4
Lesson 4 — Case study: a recent ransomware attack on a small manufacturer
Ganong Bros., St. Stephen, New Brunswick, February 2025 — what happened, what saved the company, and what the same Saturday would do to Kalmia
0:50 – 1:00
Read-aloud script — 7 minutes
Why this case
A case study is useful when the organization looks like yours. Ganong Bros., Limited, founded in 1873 in St. Stephen, New Brunswick, describes itself as Canada's original and longest-standing family-owned chocolate company — larger than Kalmia's 46, but small next to the companies that usually make the news. Like Kalmia, it produces food, ships to retailers, and depends on a short, intense season: Valentine's Day and Easter for chocolate, November and December for coffee gift boxes. The case is also unusually well documented. In August 2025 the company's head of IT (information technology) published a first-hand account in CSO Online, and the local press reported the company's statements. Everything below comes from those public sources; where they are silent, we say so.
What happened — the timeline
On the morning of Saturday, February 22, 2025, ransomware locked the company's systems. The first action was to disconnect the plant's networks from the outside world to stop the spread. Within hours, outside incident responders were on site, reviewing logs and isolated disk images, and a forensic team began analysing the ransomware. Leadership, including the Ganong family, decided not to pay. About one to two weeks later, the Play ransomware group publicly claimed the attack; according to the local press, its leak site displayed a screenshot presented as internal communications and stolen data, and the company said it was investigating whether personal information had been compromised and would notify the people concerned as privacy law requires.
By the time the ransom deadline passed, many systems had been restored from clean backups and others rebuilt. Most systems were back within about one week. Production restarted only after the machinery controllers had been checked and found free of infection, and by early March operations were back to normal. The timing could have been worse: the attack came after Valentine's Day and before Easter production. The author also notes that Ganong was one of at least 84 known incidents in the food and agriculture sector during the first quarter of 2025.
What we know about the attackers — and what we do not
Two facts are public: the attack was ransomware with double extortion, and the Play group claimed it. Following Legal Notice section 7.3, we report the claim as the sources state it. The public sources do not say how the attackers first got in. That gap is normal; most victims never publish their root cause, and an analyst must not fill it with a guess. What we can use is the official description of how this group usually operates. The joint advisory AA23-352A of CISA (Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency), the FBI (Federal Bureau of Investigation) and Australia's ACSC (Australian Cyber Security Centre), updated on June 4, 2025, reports about 900 affected organizations as of May 2025 and lists the group's usual initial access: abuse of valid accounts, external-facing services such as RDP (Remote Desktop Protocol) and VPN (virtual private network), and known vulnerabilities in public-facing products; it also describes data theft before encryption. In a threat catalogue this becomes careful wording: “threat source: ransomware group of the Play type; usual initial access according to CISA AA23-352A: valid accounts, exposed remote access, unpatched public-facing services” — not “Play got in through the VPN”.
What saved the company
The account names the decisive factor plainly: offline backups. Because a clean copy existed outside the reach of the ransomware, the company could restore instead of paying. Four other decisions mattered: isolation in the first hour, outside responders within hours, a clear decision on the ransom by the owners, and the check of production controllers before restarting the lines. The lessons the company adopted afterwards are just as concrete: written ransomware scenarios, a backup way to communicate when e-mail and phones are down, tabletop exercises for the leadership team, stricter security requirements for vendors, and sharing anonymized lessons with other companies in the sector.
The other ending — KNP Logistics
Compare a case that ended differently. In 2023, KNP Logistics, a 158-year-old transport company in England operating about 500 trucks, was hit by ransomware. According to the BBC (British Broadcasting Corporation) Panorama report of July 21, 2025, the attackers got in by guessing one employee's password; the company's data was encrypted and its systems locked; the company said its IT met industry standards and it had cyber insurance; specialists estimated the demand at up to £5 million, which it could not pay. The data could not be recovered, the company closed, and about 700 people lost their jobs. Two organizations, the same kind of attack, opposite outcomes. The difference is not the attacker; it is what the victim had prepared: a way to authenticate that a guessed password could not defeat, and a backup that the attacker could not reach.
The question for Kalmia
Now apply the case to Kalmia, using only facts from its own documents. Isolation: the roastery network is flat, so disconnecting the infected part means disconnecting everything. Backup: NAS-01's only backup disk stays plugged in, so it would be encrypted with the data. Plan and contacts: there is no incident response plan. Communication: everything runs on Microsoft 365. Production controller: ROAST-PC runs Windows 10, which stopped receiving free security updates on October 14, 2025, and is reachable by the vendor's remote-access tool with a shared password. Authentication: MFA (multi-factor authentication) protects only two accounts. Kalmia today resembles KNP more than Ganong. That sentence is not a conclusion of the risk analysis — Topics 4 to 7 will verify each fact and rate each risk — but it tells you which rows of Labs 2, 3 and 4 deserve your attention first.
Professor cue Tell the Ganong story in three minutes, chronologically, then show the KNP contrast in one minute. Ask the class: “What did Ganong have that KNP did not?” Expected answers: clean offline backups and an authentication that a guessed password could not open (for KNP, by the BBC's account). Then run Code example 4 to the gap list and stop on the cost comparison. Stress the method: public facts only, no guess about the root cause, attribution as reported.
Key terms of Lesson 4
case study
the analysis of a real, documented incident in order to draw lessons for another organization
root cause
the first weakness that made the incident possible; often not published by the victim
offline backup
a copy of data that is disconnected or immutable, so that malware on the network cannot reach or change it
isolation
disconnecting affected systems or networks to stop an attack from spreading, while keeping evidence
incident responders
specialists who contain an incident, preserve evidence and help recover
tabletop exercise
a discussion-based rehearsal in which managers walk through an incident scenario and their decisions
operational technology (OT)
computers and controllers that run physical production, such as Ganong's machinery controllers or Kalmia's ROAST-PC
attribution
naming who carried out an attack; in this course always reported as the official source states it (Legal Notice 7.3)
Micro-activity — would Kalmia survive the same Saturday? (2 min)
Three yes-or-no questions; students answer in the chat before the reveal. (1) Could Kalmia disconnect only the infected part of its network within one hour? (2) Does Kalmia have a copy of NAS-01 that ransomware on the network could not reach? (3) If e-mail and Teams were down, does every manager know how to reach the others and the IT provider?
Answer key (1) No — the roastery network is flat (Class 1 warning sign; Lab 1 network map). (2) No — the only backup disk stays connected to NAS-01. (3) No written answer exists — there is no incident response plan. Three “no” answers are three rows for Lab 3 and three candidate measures for Lab 4: segmentation, an offline or immutable backup tested every month, and an incident contact sheet kept on paper.

Real-life example — Would Kalmia survive the same Saturday? — the Ganong timeline and Kalmia's gap list
Real-life example 4 · Kalmia Coffee Roasters Inc. (fictional)
Would Kalmia survive the same Saturday? — the Ganong timeline and Kalmia's gap list
Task. Rebuild the public timeline of the Ganong Bros. incident (day, phase, event, source, certainty), extract the measures that helped the company recover and those it adopted afterwards, compare each one with Kalmia's documented state, mark each as in place, partial or missing, estimate the wholesale sales at risk with and without a usable backup, and write the gaps and the case's threat events for the labs.
How it relates to the lecture. This is the case study applied to the case organization: a real incident becomes a checklist, and every check uses a fact from Kalmia's own documents. It also practises the method of Lesson 4 — public sources only, certainty marked, no invented root cause.
Labs it prepares. Lab 2 — Threat catalogue: the case gives three threat events (ransomware on NAS-01 and its connected backup, valid-account abuse through a guessed or stolen password, data copied and published). Lab 3 — Risk register: the cost comparison is a first impact estimate for the ransomware risk. Lab 4 — Treatment plan: the missing measures (offline backup, segmentation, incident contact sheet, MFA, vendor requirements) are the first candidates.

The cost lines of the script make the gap concrete with Class 1's figure of about $9,500 of wholesale sales per day: about one working week of recovery with a clean backup (≈ $47,500 of wholesale sales at risk) against about three working weeks of rebuilding without one (≈ $142,500), before counting the cafés, the web shop or lost recipes. These are illustrations for discussion, not ratings; Lab 3 will rate impact with the scales of Topic 5.
Code example 4 — Case timeline and Kalmia gap check (Bash)
Task. A Bash script that reads the public timeline of the Ganong Bros. incident (case_timeline.csv) and Kalmia's comparison list (kalmia_vs_case.csv), prints the dated timeline with the phase and the certainty of each event, counts the measures in place, partial and missing, estimates the wholesale sales at risk for two recovery scenarios, and writes kalmia_case_gaps.csv (for Labs 3 and 4) and case_threat_events.csv (for Lab 2).
How it relates to the lecture. It turns the case study into a reusable procedure: any public incident written as a CSV (comma-separated values) timeline can be compared with Kalmia in the same way. The timeline and the checklist are drawn as the script runs.
▶ Interactive run — use Start / Pause, Step and Restart inside the window
Data files:
Show the complete commented code — case_timeline.sh (Bash; a comment line above every line of code)
Step-by-step explanation
  1. The script starts with a shebang line and set -euo pipefail, so that any failed command, unset variable or broken pipe stops it instead of producing wrong results silently.
  2. It defines the input and output file names, the discovery date (2025-02-22) and Class 1's daily wholesale figure ($9,500) as variables at the top, where they are easy to change.
  3. It reads case_timeline.csv line by line with a while-read loop and IFS (Internal Field Separator) set to the comma, converts each day offset into a calendar date with GNU (GNU's Not Unix, the free-software project that maintains the standard Linux command-line tools) date, and prints the event with its phase and certainty (stated or approximate).
  4. It reads kalmia_vs_case.csv, prints each comparison, and counts the statuses in an associative array.
  5. It computes the two cost scenarios with integer arithmetic: working days of recovery × daily wholesale sales.
  6. It writes the two output CSV files with a header line and one line per gap or threat event, then prints a summary.
  7. Start/Pause, Step and Restart replay the real recorded run line by line (GNU Bash 5 with an xtrace recorder); the drawing places each timeline event and turns each check red, amber or green. To run it yourself you need Bash and GNU date (Linux, WSL [Windows Subsystem for Linux] or Git Bash on Windows).
Run it yourself: on Linux, macOS or Windows Subsystem for Linux, put case_timeline.sh, case_timeline.csv and kalmia_vs_case.csv in one folder, open a terminal there and type bash case_timeline.sh. The script needs GNU date (standard on Linux and WSL; on macOS install coreutils and change date to gdate).
Schematic 4 — Ganong Bros. ransomware incident (February–March 2025) and Kalmia's gap list, with the KNP contrast
Top: the public timeline from discovery to restoration, by phase, with the certainty of each date. Bottom left: what saved Ganong and what it adopted afterwards. Bottom right: the same measures at Kalmia today, and the KNP contrast (guessed password, no recovery).
Animation — Why segmentation matters: one infected PC on a flat network and on a segmented network
Animation (8 steps, loops): on Kalmia's flat network one infected PC (personal computer) reaches NAS-01, the always-connected backup disk, ROAST-PC and the cameras; on a segmented network (a Lab 4 option) rules between the office segment and the server / production segment stop the spread. Segmentation plus an offline backup is the difference between recovery in days (Ganong) and closure (KNP).

Official Canadian sources
  • Canadian Centre for Cyber Security (Cyber Centre)
    Canada's national technical authority on cyber security, part of the Communications Security Establishment. Alerts, advisories, guidance for small and medium organizations, and incident reporting. https://www.cyber.gc.ca/en [VirusTotal check]
  • National Cyber Threat Assessment 2025-2026 — Canadian Centre for Cyber Security
    Canada's official assessment of who threatens Canadian organizations: state programs (China, Russia, Iran, North Korea, India), ransomware as the top cybercrime threat to critical infrastructure, cybercrime-as-a-service, hacktivists. Source of the actor descriptions in Lesson 1. https://www.cyber.gc.ca/en/guidance/national-cyber-threat-assessment-2025-2026 [VirusTotal check]
  • An introduction to the cyber threat environment — Canadian Centre for Cyber Security
    Baseline definitions of cyber threat actors, their motivations (geopolitical, financial, ideological, satisfaction, discontent) and their levels of sophistication. https://www.cyber.gc.ca/en/guidance/introduction-cyber-threat-environment [VirusTotal check]
  • Ransomware — Canadian Centre for Cyber Security
    The Cyber Centre's ransomware page: what ransomware does, how to prevent and recover, and where to report an attack in Canada. https://www.cyber.gc.ca/en/ransomware [VirusTotal check]
  • Ransomware: How to prevent and recover (ITSAP.00.099) — Cyber Centre
    Short official guide for small organizations: backups kept offline, patching, MFA (multi-factor authentication), awareness, and the first steps after an attack. https://www.cyber.gc.ca/en/guidance/ransomware-how-prevent-and-recover-itsap00099 [VirusTotal check]
  • Report a cyber incident — Canadian Centre for Cyber Security
    The official page for reporting a cyber incident to the Cyber Centre in Canada. https://www.cyber.gc.ca/en/incident-management [VirusTotal check]
  • Get Cyber Safe — Government of Canada
    The federal public-awareness campaign: plain-language pages and checklists on phishing, passwords, MFA and small-business security. https://www.getcybersafe.gc.ca/en [VirusTotal check]
  • Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre (CAFC)
    Where Canadians report fraud and scams, including business email compromise and invoice fraud such as Kalmia's INC-02. https://antifraudcentre-centreantifraude.ca/ [VirusTotal check]
  • Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP)
    Canada's federal police; its National Cybercrime Coordination Centre coordinates cybercrime investigations. https://www.rcmp.ca/en [VirusTotal check]
  • Commission d'accès à l'information du Québec (CAI)
    Québec's privacy regulator: confidentiality incidents involving personal information that present a risk of serious injury must be reported to it (relevant to Kalmia's INC-04). https://www.cai.gouv.qc.ca/ [VirusTotal check]
  • Act respecting the protection of personal information in the private sector (CQLR [Compilation of Québec Laws and Regulations], c. P-39.1) — LégisQuébec
    The Québec law (as amended by Law 25) that requires enterprises to keep a register of confidentiality incidents and to notify the CAI and the people concerned when there is a risk of serious injury. https://www.legisquebec.gouv.qc.ca/en/document/cs/P-39.1 [VirusTotal check]
Standards and frameworks
  • NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) SP (Special Publication) 800-30 Rev. 1 — Guide for Conducting Risk Assessments
    The NIST guide whose Appendix D defines threat sources (adversarial, accidental, structural, environmental) and the three characteristics of adversaries used in Lab 2: capability, intent and targeting. https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/30/r1/final [VirusTotal check]
  • NIST SP 800-83 Rev. 1 — Guide to Malware Incident Prevention and Handling for Desktops and Laptops
    The NIST guide that gives the definition of malware used in Lesson 3 and describes the main malware families and how to prevent and handle malware incidents. https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/83/r1/final [VirusTotal check]
  • NIST Computer Security Resource Center — Glossary
    Official definitions of threat, threat source, malware, phishing, social engineering, denial of service and credential terms. https://csrc.nist.gov/glossary [VirusTotal check]
  • MITRE ATT&CK (Adversarial Tactics, Techniques, and Common Knowledge)
    The public knowledge base of attacker tactics and techniques. Today you only see technique identifiers as a preview; Class 5 (Thursday) teaches how to use it. https://attack.mitre.org/ [VirusTotal check]
United States, United Kingdom and international sources
  • Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA)
    The United States federal agency for cyber and infrastructure security; publishes the #StopRansomware advisories. https://www.cisa.gov/ [VirusTotal check]
  • Defining Insider Threats — CISA
    The United States Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency's definitions of insider, insider threat and the types used in Lesson 2: unintentional (negligent, accidental), intentional (malicious), collusive and third-party. https://www.cisa.gov/defining-insider-threats [VirusTotal check]
  • #StopRansomware: Play Ransomware (AA23-352A, updated June 4, 2025) — CISA, FBI (Federal Bureau of Investigation), ASD (Australian Signals Directorate)'s ACSC (Australian Cyber Security Centre)
    Joint government advisory describing how the Play ransomware group usually gets in (valid accounts, exposed RDP [Remote Desktop Protocol] and VPN [virtual private network] services, known vulnerabilities), how it extorts victims, and the recommended mitigations. Background for Lesson 4. https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-352a [VirusTotal check]
  • Heightened DDoS (distributed denial of service) Threat Posed by Mirai and Other Botnets (TA16-288A) — CISA
    The 2016 alert about botnets built from cameras and routers that kept their factory passwords — the textbook case of opportunistic attacks (Lesson 1) and of DDoS (Lesson 3). https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/alerts/2016/10/14/heightened-ddos-threat-posed-mirai-and-other-botnets [VirusTotal check]

  • National Cyber Security Centre (United Kingdom)

  • No More Ransom
    Law-enforcement and industry project that publishes free decryption tools for some ransomware families and advice for victims. https://www.nomoreransom.org/en/index.html [VirusTotal check]

Legal and ethical notice
All work in this course uses the fictional case organization Kalmia Coffee Roasters Inc. (Torréfaction Kalmia inc.) and the lab material provided, with explicit authorization. Unauthorized access to, or interference with, computer systems is a criminal offence — for example under the Canadian Criminal Code s. 342.1, the US (United States) Computer Fraud and Abuse Act 18 U.S.C. § 1030, EU (European Union) Directive 2013/40/EU and Spain's Ley Orgánica 10/1995 — regardless of intent. Tonight's topic adds three specific rules. Threat information is studied, never acted on: you do not visit leak sites, contact threat actors or download breach data (section 7.3). Phishing, pretexting and any other social engineering directed at a real person are prohibited in every circumstance (sections 6.3 and 7.7.3); the e-mails and messages in this module are fictional training samples. Real incidents (Ganong Bros., KNP) are discussed only from public sources, and attribution to a group is reported as the source states it, not as established fact (section 7.3).
Sections of the Legal Notice that apply tonight
  • Section 6.3 and 7.7.3 — No phishing, pretexting or other social engineering directed at a real person, in any circumstance; the messages in this module are fictional samples.
  • Section 7.3 — Threat information is studied, never acted on: no leak sites, no contact with threat actors, no breach data; attribution is reported only as an official source states it.
  • Section 7.5 and 7.9 — Work only on the fictional Kalmia material and the authorized lab environment; real organizations are discussed from public sources only.
  • Section 8 — Legal warning: unauthorized access to or interference with computer systems is a criminal offence, whatever the intent.
  • Section 14.2 and Annex C — Check links and downloads (VirusTotal, Google Safe Browsing) before opening them.
  • Section 18 — Academic integrity: your lab answers are your own analysis of Kalmia; cite every source you use.
